newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Breakup not key to Russia monopoly reform - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Breakup not key to Russia monopoly reform - analysts.

text.p: Russia's natural monopolies, its largest companies and major targets for reform, do not want to be broken up, but economists said on Wednesday that dividing up the giants was not the test of reform in any case.
"It is a complete red herring," said Christopher Granville, director of research at United City Bank.
"No one in the government has ever said they are going to break up the transport structure of Gazprom, which essentially is the natural monopoly."

Analysts said newly-appointed reformers would have to audit firms or change their management to prove they meant business. "We should see action within the next two or three days on who is in charge," said Dirk Damrau, head of research at Renaissance Capital bank.
President Boris Yeltsin has given First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov the task of reforming natural monopolies, which are widely considered bloated and inefficient.
He says the government, which has huge stakes in the firms, could increase management control.

Gas producer and pipeline owner Gazprom, with well over 90 percent of production, and Unified Energy System, which controls the national electrical power grid and has stakes in local utilities and plants, are the top targets.
Leaders of the companies say they cannot be broken up and that they are trying to lead reforms from the inside.
Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev told the Duma lower house of parliament on Wednesday it would be a disaster to break up his company because it would bring higher costs for Russians.
"Proposed measures for structural reform in the gas industry...will result in the creation of monopolies in different spheres of activity which won't compete with one another," he said.

Sergei Obratsov, chief of the economy department at Unified Energy System (UES), told Reuters the company had penned its own plan for restructuring, which did not envision a breakup -- and government and industry leaders approved. "Nemtsov also supported it," he said.
He said the company, in which the government has a controlling stake, welcomed further government control.
But economists say the real battles in the short term will be about asserting that control and improving regulation.
Damrau said moves to audit the entire electricity production system, essentially controlled by UES through majority stakes in most local power utilities, would show that reformers were in control.
Changes in the UES leadership, whom Nemtsov has criticised sharply for a massive payments crisis, would also show the reformers' strength.

Lars Bergstrom, managing director of Alfred Berg investment bank in Moscow, said reforming the national electricity market and cutting cross-subsidisation, whereby industrial consumers paid high rates so households could pay low rates, would be key.
"You can have a regulated wholesale market that is owned by a company or the state and yet has a regulatory body that makes sure the market is operating efficiently," he said.

The government has already set dates for raising gas rates for households, and Granville said a timetable for household electricity price hikes would show that the government was ready to tackle necessary, but politically unpopular measures.
"That will be a test to see if (reform) will be pursued energetically," he said.
